decks.title: Introduction to Microeconomics — Part 1: Scarcity, Micro and Macro, Types of Economy
goals: Describe centrally planned, market and mixed economies

slides.heading: Economics: Scarcity and Choice
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how society chooses among **alternative uses** of scarce resources.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: scarcity and choice, micro and macro, positive and normative economics, types of economy
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every society wants more goods and services than it can produce. This part explains why that forces choices. We then separate the study of single units from the study of the whole economy, and statements of fact from statements of value. Finally we describe three types of economy: centrally planned, market and mixed.

slides.heading: Scarcity and choice
slides.body_md: **Economics** is the study of how society allocates **scarce** resources among alternative uses to satisfy wants. Resources are limited, wants are many and resources have other uses, so a **choice** must be made.

nodes.label: The next best use is given up

visual.alt: Flow from many wants and limited resources with alternative uses to choice and the opportunity cost of the next best use
visual.caption: Scarcity leads to choice

slides.narration: Economics studies how a society uses scarce resources among alternative uses to satisfy its wants. Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with wants. Because the same land, labour or funds can serve more than one purpose, using them in one way means giving up another. That is why every society has to choose.

slides.heading: Opportunity cost of a choice
slides.body_md: The **opportunity cost** of a choice is the value of the next best alternative given up. The imagined town of Halsey has one plot: building the school means that the hospital cannot be built there.

rows: No: this is the opportunity cost

visual.alt: Table of the choice of the imagined town of Halsey between a school and a hospital on one plot, the hospital being the opportunity cost of the school
visual.caption: Imagined town of Halsey, one plot.

slides.narration: The town of Halsey has one empty plot. It could hold a school or a hospital, but not both. If the town builds the school, the hospital is the next best use that is given up. This forgone alternative is the opportunity cost of the choice. Scarcity makes the cost unavoidable.

slides.body_md: **Microeconomics** studies the behaviour of individual units such as a consumer, a producer or a single market.

visual.alt: Chart comparing microeconomics, which studies individual units such as a consumer, a producer, a single market and the price of one product, with macroeconomics, which studies the economy as a whole: national income, total employment, the general price level, total savings and total output
visual.caption: Microeconomics and macroeconomics.

slides.narration: Microeconomics studies individual units. These are a single consumer, a single producer, or one market. A typical question is how the price of tablets is set in one market, or how much of a good one household buys. Macroeconomics, shown on the right of the chart, instead looks at the economy as a whole.

slides.heading: Macroeconomics
slides.body_md: **Macroeconomics** studies the economy as a whole: national income, total employment and the general price level.

headers: Topic in the imagined economy of Kelvaria
rows: Weekly demand of one household for apples
Price of tablets in one market
Output decision of one tablet factory

visual.alt: Table of six imagined topics of Kelvaria and whether each is micro or macro
visual.caption: Imagined Kelvaria.

slides.narration: Macroeconomics deals with totals and averages for the whole economy. Examples are national income, total employment and the general price level. In this table of imagined topics for Kelvaria, the demand of one household and the price of one product are micro topics. National income and the general price level are macro topics.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: micro or macro?
slides.body_md: Classify each imagined topic of the town of Halsey.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask whether the topic is about **one unit** or about the **whole economy**.
Step 2 — The price of one brand of tea and the wage of one bakery concern single units: **micro**.
Step 3 — Total output and total employment of Halsey concern the whole economy: **macro**.

rows: Price of one brand of tea in a Halsey shop
Total output of all goods in Halsey

visual.alt: Worked classification of four imagined topics of Halsey into micro and macro
visual.caption: Imagined town of Halsey.

slides.narration: To classify a topic, ask whether it concerns one unit or the whole economy. The price of one brand of tea in a shop and the wage paid by one bakery concern single units, so they are micro topics. Total output and total employment of the whole town describe the entire economy, so they are macro topics.

slides.heading: Quick check: micro topic
slides.body_md: Pick the microeconomics topic from an imagined list.
slides.narration: Look at each option and ask whether it concerns a single market, firm or household, or the economy as a whole. Choose the option that concerns a single unit. Remember that national income, total employment and the general price level belong to the other branch.

slides.heading: Positive economics
slides.body_md: **Positive economics** deals with what **is**: statements that can be tested against facts. A positive statement may be true or false.

rows: Apple output in Kelvaria fell after the frost
Compare output figures before and after
The price of cloth in Tarvania is higher than the price of wheat per kilogram
Unemployment in Orlin rose last year

visual.alt: Table of three imagined positive statements and how each can be tested with facts
visual.caption: Positive statements can be true or false.

slides.narration: Positive economics describes what is. A positive statement can be tested against facts, such as output figures, prices or employment records. It may turn out to be true or false, but it can always be checked. The table gives imagined examples and the data that would test each of them.

slides.heading: Normative economics
slides.body_md: **Normative economics** deals with what **ought to be**. A normative statement rests on a value judgement, so facts alone cannot settle it.

rows: Kelvaria ought to give every school a tablet
Value judgement about what should be done
It is unfair that a few families own most orchards
Tarvania should tax luxury cloth heavily

visual.alt: Table of three imagined normative statements and why each rests on a value judgement
visual.caption: Normative statements express what ought to be.

slides.narration: Normative economics deals with what ought to be. Its statements contain value judgements, often with words such as should, ought or unfair. Facts can inform the debate, but they cannot by themselves decide it, because people differ in what they value. The table gives imagined normative statements and the reason each is normative.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: positive or normative?
slides.body_md: Classify four imagined statements about Tarvania and Belmora.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask whether the statement can be **tested** with facts.
Step 2 — Look for judgement words such as **should** and **ought**.
Step 3 — Facts about output or prices: positive. Judgements about policy: normative.

rows: Cloth output in Tarvania rose last year
Tarvania should reduce its cloth imports
The price of rice in Belmora is lower in autumn
Belmora ought to subsidise rice farmers

visual.alt: Worked classification of four imagined statements about Tarvania and Belmora as positive or normative
visual.caption: Look for facts that can be tested, or for words such as should and ought.

slides.narration: To classify a statement, ask whether facts can test it. A claim that cloth output rose, or that rice is cheaper in autumn, can be checked, so it is positive. A claim that a country should cut imports or ought to help farmers contains a value judgement, so it is normative.

slides.heading: Quick check: positive statement
slides.body_md: Pick the positive statement from an imagined list.
slides.narration: Read each statement and ask whether it can be tested against facts. Statements with words like should, ought or unfair express judgements. The positive statement describes something that happened or exists and can be checked against data.

slides.heading: Using both kinds of statement
slides.body_md: A sound policy decision uses **positive** analysis to find the facts and **normative** judgement to decide what ought to be done.

nodes.label: Normative: judge what ought to be done

visual.alt: Flow from positive facts to normative judgement to a policy decision that uses both
visual.caption: Facts and values together

slides.narration: In practice both kinds of statement are needed. Positive analysis finds out what is happening and what a policy would do. Normative judgement then decides whether that outcome is desirable. A policy decision uses the two together: the facts come first, and the values decide what to do about them.

slides.heading: Centrally planned economy
slides.body_md: In a **centrally planned economy** the government or a central authority decides what, how and for whom to produce, through a plan.

nodes.label: Plan for what, how and for whom

visual.alt: Flow of decisions in a centrally planned economy from the central authority to its plan, allocation of resources and sharing of output
visual.caption: Centrally planned economy

slides.narration: In a centrally planned economy, a central authority takes the main decisions. It prepares a plan that says what to produce, how to produce it and for whom. Resources are allocated according to the plan, and the output is shared according to the plan as well. Prices play a limited role in these decisions.

slides.heading: Market economy
slides.body_md: In a **market economy** decisions are taken by buyers and sellers through **markets and prices**: firms follow profit, consumers follow their incomes.

visual.alt: Flow of decisions in a market economy from household incomes and demand to price and profit signals and the decisions of firms
visual.caption: Market economy

slides.narration: In a market economy, households and firms take the decisions. Households with incomes show their wants through demand in markets. Prices and profits send signals to firms, which decide what to produce and how. No central authority prepares a plan; markets guide the allocation of resources.

slides.heading: Mixed economy
slides.body_md: A **mixed economy** combines the two: private firms work through markets while the government also produces and regulates.

rows: Government or central authority, through a plan
Buyers and sellers, through markets and prices
Both: private firms through markets and the government

visual.alt: Table of the three types of economy, who takes the central decisions in each and an imagined example
visual.caption: Three imagined economies.

slides.narration: A mixed economy has both a private sector and a public sector. Private firms respond to markets and prices, while the government provides services, runs some enterprises and regulates the rest. This table compares who takes the central decisions in each of the three types, with an imagined example of each.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which type of economy?
slides.body_md: Identify the type of each imagined economy.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask **who decides** what, how and for whom to produce.
Step 2 — A state agency issues orders for every farm and factory: **centrally planned**.
Step 3 — Firms follow profit at market prices: **market**. Private shops with a state-run railway: **mixed**.

rows: A state agency tells every farm and factory in Orlin what to produce
Firms in Quillon produce whatever earns profit at market prices
Dunmere has private shops and a state-run railway

visual.alt: Worked classification of three imagined situations into centrally planned, market and mixed economies
visual.caption: Who decides?

slides.narration: To identify an economy, ask who takes the central decisions. In Orlin a state agency tells every farm and factory what to produce, so it is centrally planned. In Quillon firms follow profit at market prices, so it is a market economy. Dunmere has private shops and a state railway, so it is mixed.

slides.heading: Quick check: types of economy
slides.body_md: Match each term with its description.
slides.narration: Match the planned economy with the central authority taking decisions, the market economy with decisions through prices, the mixed economy with both sectors working, and scarcity with limited resources compared with wants. Take each description in turn.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Limited resources, many wants: choice is unavoidable
Individual units and the economy as a whole
What is, which can be tested, and what ought to be, a value judgement

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: scarcity, micro and macro, positive and normative, types of economy

slides.narration: To recap. Scarcity means limited resources and many wants, so every society must choose, and the next best alternative given up is the opportunity cost. Microeconomics studies individual units and macroeconomics the whole economy. Positive statements describe what is and can be tested. Normative statements express what ought to be. Economies are centrally planned, market or mixed.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define **scarcity**, **opportunity cost** and **economics** in the standard words.
For micro and macro, give an **example of each** and say whether it concerns a unit or the whole.
To classify a statement, say **testable** or **value judgement**, and give the reason.
Describe each type of economy by **who takes the central decisions**.
A positive statement can be **false**; it is still positive.
slides.narration: Some tips. Define scarcity and opportunity cost in the standard words. For micro and macro, always give an example and say whether it concerns a single unit or the whole economy. When you classify a statement, name the reason: testable or value judgement. Describe each type of economy by who takes the central decisions. Remember that a positive statement can be false.

goals: State the three central problems of an economy
Define opportunity cost and the production possibility frontier
Compute the marginal rate of transformation from a schedule and explain the concave shape
Explain points inside and outside the frontier and shifts of the frontier

slides.heading: Central Problems and the Frontier
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **what, how and for whom**, and the **production possibility frontier**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the central problems, opportunity cost, the production possibility frontier, the marginal rate of transformation and shifts
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Because resources are scarce, every economy must solve the same central problems. In this part we name them, and then study a simple picture that shows the choice: the production possibility frontier. We compute the cost of one good in terms of another from a schedule, and see what shifts the frontier.

slides.heading: The three central problems
slides.body_md: Scarcity forces every economy to decide **what** to produce and in what quantities, **how** to produce it, and **for whom** to produce.

visual.alt: Flow chart: scarce resources and many wants force choices, which give rise to three central problems: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce
visual.caption: The three central problems of an economy.

slides.narration: Scarce resources and many wants create choices. The first problem is what to produce, meaning which goods and how much of each. The second is how to produce, meaning the choice of technique. The third is for whom to produce, meaning how the output is shared among the people of the economy.

slides.heading: How to produce: choice of technique
slides.body_md: A good can be made with different mixes of inputs. A **labour-intensive** technique uses more labour; a **capital-intensive** technique uses more machines.

rows: Harvesting a field with 40 hired workers
Harvesting the same field with a rented machine

visual.alt: Table of the labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques with an imagined harvesting example
visual.caption: The choice of technique.

slides.narration: The second central problem is how to produce. The same good can be produced with a technique that uses more labour or one that uses more machines. A labour-intensive technique relies mainly on workers. A capital-intensive technique relies mainly on machines. The producer chooses the technique that suits the cost and the output.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing a technique
slides.body_md: Farmer Dilbag of the imagined village of Bhavpur can harvest his field with workers or with a rented machine.
bullets: Step 1 — Labour-intensive: 40 × 5 × 400 = **Rs 80,000**.
Step 2 — Capital-intensive: 2 × 30000 = **Rs 60,000**.
Step 3 — The machine is cheaper by 80000 − 60000 = **Rs 20,000**.

visual.alt: Table of the cost of harvesting the imagined field of Dilbag with workers, Rs 80,000, and with a machine, Rs 60,000, a difference of Rs 20,000
visual.caption: Imagined farmer Dilbag of Bhavpur.

slides.narration: Dilbag compares the cost of two techniques. Forty workers for five days at four hundred rupees a day cost eighty thousand rupees. A machine hired for two days at thirty thousand rupees a day costs sixty thousand. The capital-intensive technique is cheaper by twenty thousand rupees, so cost points to the machine.

slides.heading: For whom to produce
slides.body_md: **For whom to produce** is the problem of how the output is **distributed** among the members of the economy.

visual.alt: Flow from production of output to incomes earned, to who can buy and to the distribution of output
visual.caption: For whom to produce

slides.narration: The third central problem is for whom to produce. Once output is produced, it must be shared among people. Those with higher incomes can buy more of it. So how incomes are earned and distributed decides who receives the goods and services, which is the distribution of output.

slides.heading: Quick check: how to produce
slides.body_md: Identify the central problem in an imagined harvesting choice.
slides.narration: Read the situation carefully. The farmer must choose between workers and a machine for the same task. Decide whether this is about which goods to make, about the method of making them, or about who receives the output. Pick the matching central problem.

slides.heading: Opportunity cost
slides.body_md: **Opportunity cost** is the value of the **next best alternative** forgone when a choice is made.

visual.alt: Table of the incomes from three uses of Dilbag's land: sugarcane 60000 chosen, paddy 52000 as the next best and so the opportunity cost, vegetables 48000
visual.caption: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives.

slides.narration: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up. Dilbag has two hectares and can grow sugarcane, paddy or vegetables. He chooses sugarcane. The best alternative he gives up is paddy, so the opportunity cost is the income from paddy. It is not the total of all other uses.

slides.heading: The production possibility frontier
slides.body_md: The **production possibility frontier** (production possibility curve) shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with **given resources and technology**, fully and efficiently used.

rows: The quantity of resources does not change
The methods of production do not change
No resource is idle or wasted
Resources not equally efficient in both goods
Some suit one good better than the other

visual.alt: Table of the four assumptions behind the production possibility frontier
visual.caption: Production possibility frontier: combinations of two goods producible with given resources and technology.

slides.narration: The production possibility frontier shows the combinations of two goods that an economy can produce when its resources and technology are given and are used fully and efficiently. It rests on four assumptions: fixed resources, given technology, full and efficient use, and resources that are not equally efficient in producing both goods.

slides.heading: A production possibility schedule
slides.body_md: Imagine Tarvania, which uses all its resources to make wheat and cloth. Each combination uses resources fully.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined production possibilities of Tarvania: wheat 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 lakh tonnes with cloth 160, 150, 120, 70, 0 thousand metres at combinations A to E
visual.caption: Imagined Tarvania.

slides.narration: This is an imagined schedule for Tarvania. At combination A the economy makes only cloth. As it moves to B, C, D and E, it makes more wheat and less cloth. At E it makes only wheat. Every combination uses all resources fully and efficiently, so each one lies on the frontier.

slides.heading: Drawing the frontier
slides.body_md: Plot wheat on the horizontal axis and cloth on the vertical axis. Points **on** the curve are efficient; **inside** means underuse; **outside** is unattainable.

slides.heading: On, inside and outside the frontier
slides.body_md: At 2 lakh tonnes of wheat the frontier gives 120 thousand metres of cloth.

visual.alt: Table of three points of Tarvania against the frontier: C on it, U inside it by 30 and W outside it by 30
visual.caption: Imagined Tarvania.

slides.narration: At two lakh tonnes of wheat the frontier gives one hundred and twenty thousand metres of cloth. A point at ninety thousand metres is inside, with thirty thousand metres of cloth idle. A point at three lakh tonnes of wheat and one hundred thousand metres of cloth is outside, because the frontier allows only seventy. Inside means unemployment or waste.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: marginal rate of transformation
slides.body_md: The **marginal rate of transformation (MRT)**, or marginal opportunity cost, is the units of one good given up to produce one more unit of the other: MRT = ΔY ÷ ΔX.
bullets: Step 1 — A to B: cloth falls by 10, wheat rises by 1: MRT = 10 ÷ 1 = **10**.
Step 3 — The marginal rate rises at every move: 10, 30, 50, 70.

visual.alt: Table of the marginal rate of transformation of Tarvania for each move from A to E: 10, 30, 50, 70, rising at every move
visual.caption: Imagined Tarvania.

slides.narration: Divide the cloth given up by the wheat gained for each move. From A to B, ten thousand metres of cloth are given up for one lakh tonnes of wheat. Then the rate is thirty, then fifty, then seventy. The marginal rate of transformation rises at every move, so each extra lakh tonnes of wheat costs more cloth.

slides.heading: Why the frontier is concave
slides.body_md: The marginal rate rises because resources are **not equally efficient** in producing both goods. Increasing marginal opportunity cost makes the frontier **concave to the origin**.

slides.heading: Shifts of the frontier
slides.body_md: More resources or better technology shift the frontier **rightward**: growth. Destruction of resources shifts it **leftward**.

visual.alt: Shifts of the production possibility frontier of the imagined economy of Tarvania: the original curve, a dashed curve to the right after growth of resources or better technology, and a dashed curve to the left after destruction of resources
visual.caption: Imagined Tarvania. Old frontier: 160 thousand metres of cloth or 4 lakh tonnes of wheat. After growth: 200 or 5. After an earthquake: 120 or 3.

slides.narration: The frontier shifts when resources or technology change. If resources increase or technology improves, the frontier shifts to the right, and the economy can produce more of both goods. When a flood or earthquake wipes out resources, the frontier moves to the left. These shifts show growth and loss of capacity.

slides.heading: Rotation of the frontier
slides.body_md: When technology improves for **one good only**, the frontier **rotates**: that good's intercept moves out, and the other stays the same.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: gain from growth
slides.body_md: After growth, Tarvania's frontier is farther out. Find the gain in cloth capacity at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat.
bullets: Step 1 — New frontier at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat: **168** thousand metres.
Step 2 — Old frontier at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat: **120** thousand metres.
Step 3 — Gain = 168 − 120 = **48** thousand metres.

slides.narration: At two lakh tonnes of wheat, the new frontier allows one hundred sixty eight thousand metres of cloth, while the old one allowed one hundred twenty. The gain is forty eight thousand metres. The table shows that the gain differs at each level of wheat, because the new frontier lies farther out everywhere.

slides.body_md: Decide where an imagined combination lies.
slides.narration: Find the cloth that the frontier allows at the given wheat output. Compare it with the cloth actually produced. If the economy makes less than the frontier allows, the point lies inside. If it makes more, the point lies outside.

slides.heading: The frontier and the central problems
slides.body_md: The frontier shows **what to produce** as a choice of point, **efficiency** as a point on the curve, **opportunity cost** as a move along it, and **growth** as a shift outward.

rows: Choice of one point among the many on the curve
What to produce, and in what quantities
Point inside: unemployed or wasted resources
Opportunity cost: giving up one good for the other

visual.alt: Table of what the production possibility frontier shows and the central problem or idea each relates to

slides.narration: The frontier puts the central ideas into one picture. Choosing a point on the curve is the problem of what to produce. Being inside the curve shows wasted resources. Moving along the curve shows opportunity cost. A shift outward shows growth. How to produce and for whom to produce are not shown directly.

slides.heading: Quick check: shift of the frontier
slides.body_md: Decide how an earthquake affects the frontier.
slides.narration: Think about what the disaster does to the resources of the economy. Does it add to them, leave them as they are or reduce them? Then decide whether the maximum possible output of both goods rises or falls, and choose the shift that matches.

Compute **MRT = ΔY ÷ ΔX** step by step, and say whether it **rises**.
Explain concavity with **increasing marginal opportunity cost**, not just the shape.
For a point, compare it with the frontier: **on, inside or outside**.
Name the cause of each shift: **growth, destruction or one-sided technology**.

sections.heading: 1. Scarcity and choice
sections.body_md:
**Economics** studies how society allocates scarce resources among alternative uses to satisfy wants. **Scarcity** means that resources are limited relative to wants. Because resources have alternative uses, using them in one way means giving up another use, so a **choice** must be made.

The value of the next best alternative given up is the **opportunity cost** of a choice. For the imagined farmer Dilbag of Bhavpur, who grows sugarcane worth Rs 60,000 when paddy would give Rs 52,000 and vegetables Rs 48,000, the opportunity cost is Rs 52,000, the income from paddy.

key_terms.definition_md: The study of how society allocates scarce resources among alternative uses to satisfy wants.
The limited availability of resources compared with the wants to be satisfied.
The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.

nodes.label: The next best use is given up

visuals.caption: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives.

sections.heading: 2. Microeconomics and macroeconomics
sections.body_md: **Microeconomics** studies the behaviour of individual units: a consumer, a producer or a single market, for example how the price of one product is determined. **Macroeconomics** studies the economy as a whole: national income, total employment, total output and the general price level.

key_terms.definition_md: The branch of economics that studies individual economic units such as a consumer, a producer or a market.
The branch of economics that studies the economy as a whole, through aggregates such as national income, total employment and the general price level.

sections.heading: 3. Positive and normative economics
sections.body_md: **Positive economics** deals with what is. Its statements can be tested against facts and may be true or false. **Normative economics** deals with what ought to be. sections.heading: 4. Types of economy
sections.body_md: In a **centrally planned economy** the government or central authority decides what, how and for whom to produce, through a plan. In a **market economy** these decisions are taken by buyers and sellers through markets and prices. A **mixed economy** combines the two: private firms and the government both take part in production. Every economy must solve the same central problems; the types differ in who takes the decisions.

sections.heading: 5. Central problems of an economy
sections.body_md:
Scarcity gives rise to three central problems.

**What to produce, and in what quantities:** the choice of goods and how much of each.

**How to produce:** the choice of technique, **labour-intensive** (more labour) or **capital-intensive** (more machines). The imagined harvest of Dilbag costs Rs 80,000 with workers and Rs 60,000 with a machine.

**For whom to produce:** the distribution of output among the members of the economy.

key_terms.definition_md: A technique of production that uses relatively more labour than capital.
A technique of production that uses relatively more capital than labour.

sections.heading: 6. The production possibility frontier
sections.body_md:
The **production possibility frontier** (also called the production possibility curve) shows the combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with given resources and technology, when the resources are fully and efficiently used. It assumes fixed resources, given technology, full and efficient use, and resources that are not equally efficient in producing both goods.

Points **on** the curve are efficient. Points **inside** show unemployment or inefficient use of resources: at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat the imagined Tarvania frontier gives 120 thousand metres of cloth, so 90 is inside by 30. Points **outside** are unattainable.

key_terms.definition_md: The curve showing the combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with given resources and technology, using them fully and efficiently.

sections.heading: 7. Marginal rate of transformation and shifts
sections.body_md:
The **marginal rate of transformation (MRT)**, or marginal opportunity cost, is the units of one good given up to produce one more unit of the other: **MRT = ΔY ÷ ΔX**. For Tarvania the rates are 10, 30, 50, 70, rising along the frontier. The frontier is **concave to the origin** because the marginal opportunity cost rises: resources are not equally efficient in producing both goods.

The frontier shifts **right** with more resources or better technology (growth), **left** with destruction of resources such as an earthquake or flood, and **rotates** when technology improves for one good only. The frontier can also illustrate unemployment (a point inside), growth (a shift) and the central problems.

key_terms.definition_md: The units of one good that must be given up to produce one more unit of the other good, ΔY ÷ ΔX.
Another name for the marginal rate of transformation.

cards.front_md: Why is the frontier **concave** to the origin?
cards.back_md: The marginal opportunity cost rises because resources are not equally efficient in both goods.

cards.front_md: When is the frontier a **straight line**?
cards.back_md: When the marginal opportunity cost is constant, as if resources were equally efficient in both goods.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best defines economics as studied in the imagined country of Tarvania and everywhere else?

options.text_md: The study of how to earn the largest possible profit in a business
The study of how society allocates scarce resources among alternative uses to satisfy wants
The study of money, banks and the stock market alone
The study of how the government collects taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The study of how society allocates scarce resources among alternative uses to satisfy wants. Economics is concerned with the choices that arise because resources are limited while wants are many and the resources have alternative uses. Profit, money and banking, and taxation are only parts of what economics deals with.

questions.stem_md: The citizens of the imagined town of Halsey want more parks, schools and roads than the town can build. In economics this situation is called

options.text_md: plenty, because every want can be met
inflation, because prices have risen
unemployment, because workers are idle
scarcity, because resources are limited relative to wants

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** scarcity, because resources are limited relative to wants. Scarcity means that the resources available are limited compared with the wants to be satisfied. Plenty is the opposite situation, and inflation and unemployment describe prices and jobs, not the gap between wants and resources.

questions.stem_md: Why does the imagined island economy of Marrow have to make choices?

options.text_md: Its resources are limited, they have alternative uses and wants are many
Its government has decided to restrict production
Its people do not want any goods
Its resources can be used for only one purpose

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Its resources are limited, they have alternative uses and wants are many. Choice is forced by scarcity combined with alternative uses of resources: using a resource in one way means not using it in another. Where resources have only one use, or people want nothing, no choice would arise, and a government order is not the root cause.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a topic of microeconomics in the imagined economy of Kelvaria?

options.text_md: The total employment in the whole of Kelvaria
The general price level of Kelvaria
How the price of tablets is fixed in one market
The national income of Kelvaria

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** How the price of tablets is fixed in one market. Microeconomics studies individual units such as a consumer, a producer or a single market, so the price of one product in one market is a micro topic. Total employment, the general price level and national income describe the economy as a whole and belong to macroeconomics.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a topic of macroeconomics in the imagined economy of Belmora?

options.text_md: The weekly demand of one household for rice
The output decision of one steel factory
The general level of prices of all goods in Belmora
The price of one brand of tea in a village shop

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The general level of prices of all goods in Belmora. Macroeconomics deals with aggregates such as the general price level. A household, a single factory and one brand in one shop are individual units, so they belong to microeconomics.

questions.stem_md: Which of these imagined statements is a positive statement?

options.text_md: Apple output in Kelvaria fell last year after a severe frost
Kelvaria should give free tablets to every school
It is unfair that rich households own most of the orchards
The rich of Kelvaria ought to pay a higher tax

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Apple output in Kelvaria fell last year after a severe frost. A positive statement describes what is and can be checked against facts, such as the fall of apple output after a frost. The others contain words such as should, unfair and ought, which are value judgements and therefore normative.

questions.stem_md: Which of these imagined statements is a normative statement?

options.text_md: The number of libraries in Tarvania rose last year
The price of cloth in Tarvania is lower than the price of wheat per kilogram
Cloth output in Tarvania is larger than steel output
Tarvania ought to spend more on public libraries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Tarvania ought to spend more on public libraries. Ought to expresses a value judgement about what should be done, so the first statement is normative. The other three can be tested with data and are therefore positive, whether they turn out true or false.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly describes positive and normative economics?

options.text_md: Positive deals with what ought to be; normative deals with what is
Positive deals with what is and can be tested; normative deals with what ought to be and rests on value judgements
Positive deals with the whole economy; normative deals with one firm
Positive is always true; normative is always false

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Positive deals with what is and can be tested; normative deals with what ought to be and rests on value judgements. The first option states the standard distinction. The second reverses it, the third confuses it with the micro and macro divide, and a positive statement can also be false while a normative statement is neither true nor false by facts alone.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Orlin a central authority decides what, how and for whom to produce, and most resources are owned by the state. Orlin is best described as

options.text_md: a centrally planned economy
a market economy
a mixed economy
a closed economy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a centrally planned economy. When the government makes the central decisions through a plan, the economy is centrally planned. A market economy leaves decisions to markets and prices, and a mixed economy combines the two.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Quillon, producers decide what to make by watching prices and profits, and consumers decide what to buy with their incomes. This is the main feature of

options.text_md: a centrally planned economy
a market economy
a subsistence economy
a command economy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a market economy. In a market economy decisions are made by buyers and sellers through markets and prices. A central plan, a command system and a subsistence economy do not describe decisions guided by prices and profit.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Dunmere, private firms produce most consumer goods while the government runs railways and provides basic schooling. Dunmere is an example of

options.text_md: a centrally planned economy
a pure market economy
a mixed economy
a barter economy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a mixed economy. A mixed economy has both a private sector working through markets and a public sector that the government runs. A planned economy would leave nothing to private firms, and a pure market economy would have no state role.

questions.stem_md: The government of the imagined country of Kelvaria must decide whether to use its farmland for apples or for tablet factories and how much of each to make. This is the central problem of

options.text_md: how to produce
for whom to produce
how to reduce prices
what to produce and in what quantities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** what to produce and in what quantities. Choosing which goods and how much of each to produce is the problem of what to produce. How to produce concerns the technique, and for whom concerns the distribution of output among people.

questions.stem_md: Farmer Dilbag of the imagined village of Bhavpur must decide whether to harvest his wheat with forty hired workers or with a rented harvesting machine. This is the central problem of

options.text_md: what to produce
for whom to produce
whom to employ for life
how to produce, the choice of technique

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** how to produce, the choice of technique. Choosing between a labour-intensive and a capital-intensive method is the choice of technique, which is the problem of how to produce. What to produce is about the product, and for whom is about who receives the output.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Belmora, steel and rice are produced. The question of how this output will be shared among households is the problem of

options.text_md: what to produce
how to produce
for whom to produce, the distribution of output
how to import goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** for whom to produce, the distribution of output. Sharing the output among the members of society is the problem of for whom to produce. What to produce and how to produce deal with the choice of goods and of technique.

questions.stem_md: A production possibility frontier shows

options.text_md: the combinations of two goods that consumers prefer
the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources and technology when they are fully and efficiently used
the price at which two goods are sold in a market
the growth of national income over several years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources and technology when they are fully and efficiently used. The frontier is a boundary of what can be produced with given resources and technology. It is not about consumer preference, market prices or growth over time, although a shift of the frontier is used to show growth.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT an assumption behind the production possibility frontier of an imagined economy?

options.text_md: Resources and technology keep changing every year
Resources are fully and efficiently used
Technology is given
Resources are not equally efficient in producing both goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Resources and technology keep changing every year. The frontier is drawn for fixed resources and a given technology, so constant change in them is not an assumption; if they change, the frontier shifts. The other three are assumptions of the usual PPF.

questions.stem_md: Tarvania produces wheat and cloth and its frontier passes through 2 lakh tonnes of wheat and 120 thousand metres of cloth. The economy is producing 2 lakh tonnes of wheat and 90 thousand metres of cloth. This combination

options.text_md: lies on the frontier, showing full and efficient use
lies inside the frontier, showing that resources are not fully or efficiently used
lies outside the frontier and cannot be produced
lies on the wheat axis

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** lies inside the frontier, showing that resources are not fully or efficiently used. At 2 lakh tonnes of wheat the frontier gives 120 thousand metres of cloth, which is 30 more than 90. So the point is below the frontier: it is attainable but some resources are idle or badly used. A point on the frontier would show 120, and a point outside would show more than 120.

questions.stem_md: Tarvania can produce at most 70 thousand metres of cloth when it makes 3 lakh tonnes of wheat. A plan to produce 3 lakh tonnes of wheat and 100 thousand metres of cloth would be

options.text_md: attainable by moving inside the frontier
efficient and attainable
possible only in a centrally planned economy
unattainable with the present resources and technology

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** unattainable with the present resources and technology. The frontier gives 70 thousand metres at 3 lakh tonnes of wheat, and 100 exceeds it by 30. A point outside the frontier cannot be reached with given resources and technology, whatever the type of economy.

questions.stem_md: The production possibility curve of an imagined economy is concave to the origin because

options.text_md: the marginal opportunity cost rises as more of a good is produced
the marginal opportunity cost falls as more of a good is produced
the marginal opportunity cost is the same at every point
the economy always uses its resources fully

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the marginal opportunity cost rises as more of a good is produced. Resources are not equally efficient in all uses, so the first units of a good use the resources best suited to it and later units need less suitable resources, which raises the opportunity cost. Constant cost gives a straight line and falling cost a curve bowed toward the origin; full use of resources is an assumption, not the reason for the shape.

questions.stem_md: Farmer Dilbag can use his two hectares for sugarcane (income Rs 60,000), paddy (Rs 52,000) or vegetables (Rs 48,000). He plants sugarcane. His opportunity cost is

options.text_md: Rs 60,000, the income from sugarcane
Rs 1,00,000, the income from both other crops
Rs 52,000, the income from the next best alternative, paddy
Rs 48,000, the income from the least valuable use

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rs 52,000, the income from the next best alternative, paddy. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, which is paddy at Rs 52,000. The income from sugarcane is what he gains, not what he gives up; adding both alternatives, or using the lowest, does not measure the next best use.

questions.stem_md: The marginal rate of transformation between two goods X and Y, with X on the horizontal axis, is

options.text_md: the units of X given up to produce one more unit of Y only
the total output of X and Y together
the units of Y given up to produce one more unit of X, that is ΔY / ΔX
the price of X divided by the price of Y

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the units of Y given up to produce one more unit of X, that is ΔY / ΔX. MRT, also called marginal opportunity cost, is the loss of one good per unit gained of the other, ΔY ÷ ΔX. It is not a total output and is not a ratio of prices.

questions.stem_md: The production possibility frontier of the imagined economy of Lumeria shifts to the right when

options.text_md: its resources increase or its technology improves
a flood destroys many factories
it moves from a point on the frontier to a point inside it
its people start to want different goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** its resources increase or its technology improves. More resources or better technology raise what the economy can produce, so the frontier moves outward. A flood shifts it inward, a move to an inside point is not a shift, and a change in wants does not alter productive capacity.

questions.stem_md: A severe earthquake destroys many factories and farms of the imagined economy of Orlin. The production possibility frontier of Orlin will

options.text_md: shift to the right
rotate with one intercept unchanged
remain unchanged
shift to the left

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** shift to the left. Destruction of resources lowers the maximum output of both goods, so the whole frontier shifts inward, to the left. The frontier shifts right with growth, rotates when technology improves for one good only, and cannot stay unchanged when capacity is destroyed.

questions.stem_md: Better technology is introduced only in the cloth industry of Tarvania, while wheat technology does not change. The frontier of wheat and cloth

options.text_md: shifts inward in parallel
rotates outward, the cloth intercept rising and the wheat intercept unchanged
rotates inward on the cloth axis
shifts outward in parallel at both axes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** rotates outward, the cloth intercept rising and the wheat intercept unchanged. The maximum output of cloth rises while the maximum output of wheat stays the same, so the curve swings out on the cloth axis only. An inward shift needs lower capacity, and a parallel outward shift needs improvement in both goods.

questions.stem_md: Kelvaria gives up tablets as it moves along its frontier: A: 0 hundred tonnes of apples, 100 thousand tablets; B: 5 hundred tonnes of apples, 95 thousand tablets; C: 10 hundred tonnes of apples, 85 thousand tablets; D: 15 hundred tonnes of apples, 70 thousand tablets; E: 20 hundred tonnes of apples, 50 thousand tablets. Which statement about the marginal rate of transformation is correct?

options.text_md: It rises from 1 to 4 thousand tablets per hundred tonnes of apples
It stays at 1 at every step
It falls from 4 to 1
It is zero at point A

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It rises from 1 to 4 thousand tablets per hundred tonnes of apples. Between consecutive points the tablets given up are 5, 10, 15, 20 for 5 hundred tonnes of apples each, so the marginal rate is 1, 2, 3, 4: it rises. It is neither constant nor falling.

questions.stem_md: The imagined economy of Dorvik produces wheat and rice with the schedule A: 0 thousand bags of wheat, 60 thousand bags of rice; B: 10 thousand bags of wheat, 40 thousand bags of rice; C: 20 thousand bags of wheat, 20 thousand bags of rice; D: 30 thousand bags of wheat, 0 thousand bags of rice. Its frontier is a straight line. This means that

options.text_md: the marginal opportunity cost rises at every step
the marginal opportunity cost is constant at 2 thousand bags of rice per thousand bags of wheat, as if resources were equally efficient in both uses
the economy has unemployed resources
the frontier is concave to the origin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the marginal opportunity cost is constant at 2 thousand bags of rice per thousand bags of wheat, as if resources were equally efficient in both uses. Each step of 10 thousand bags of wheat costs 20 thousand bags of rice, so the rate is 2 throughout. This is the case only when resources are equally efficient in both goods. Idle resources would put the economy inside the line, and a concave curve needs rising cost.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The production possibility curve of an economy that makes steel and rice is concave to the origin.

**Reason (R):** Resources are not equally efficient in producing steel and rice, so giving up more rice is needed to obtain each extra unit of steel.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. Because resources differ in how well they suit each good, the opportunity cost rises along the frontier, which gives the concave shape.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An improvement in technology shifts the production possibility frontier of an economy outward.

**Reason (R):** The production possibility frontier is concave to the origin.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. Better technology raises the maximum output and moves the frontier out; the concave shape is the effect of increasing marginal opportunity cost and has nothing to do with the shift.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Along the frontier of a typical economy, the marginal rate of transformation rises as more of one good is produced.

**Reason (R):** Resources are equally efficient in the production of both goods.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: it is because resources are not equally efficient in both goods that the marginal opportunity cost rises. Equal efficiency would give a constant rate and a straight-line frontier.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A point inside the production possibility frontier shows that resources are fully and efficiently used.

**Reason (R):** A point inside the frontier can be produced with the given resources and technology.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: an inside point means that some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently. R is true, because inside points are attainable, but this does not make them efficient.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A positive statement of economics must always be true.

**Reason (R):** A positive statement is one that can be tested against facts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: a positive statement can be false, as when a claim about prices is checked and found wrong. R is true, since testability against facts is what makes a statement positive, whether it turns out true or false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The output decision of a single steel factory in the imagined economy of Belmora is a topic of macroeconomics.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The decision of one producer is a micro topic; macroeconomics deals with aggregates such as national income and total employment.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A normative statement, such as the claim that Quillon should reduce its inequality, can be proved right or wrong by facts alone.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A normative statement contains a value judgement about what ought to be. Facts can inform the debate but cannot settle it alone.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Tarvania can reach a point outside its present frontier by using its existing resources and technology more efficiently.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Efficient use of resources only takes the economy to the frontier. A point outside needs more resources or better technology.

questions.solution_md: The choice of technique belongs to the problem of how to produce.

Find the marginal rate of transformation when the economy moves from B to C.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Wheat rises from 1 to 2, so ΔX = 1 lakh tonnes.
Step 2: Cloth falls from 150 to 120, so ΔY = 30 thousand metres.
Step 3: MRT = 30 ÷ 1 = 30.

Step 2: The cloth given up is 70 − 0 = 70 thousand metres, which is the opportunity cost of the fourth lakh tonne of wheat.

Step 1: Cloth at B is 150 and at D is 70.
Step 2: Cloth given up = 150 − 70 = 80 thousand metres. As a check, the two marginal losses 30 and 50 add to 80.

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 80 thousand metres of cloth

questions.stem_md: The Tarvania schedule is A: 0 lakh tonnes of wheat, 160 thousand metres of cloth; B: 1 lakh tonnes of wheat, 150 thousand metres of cloth; C: 2 lakh tonnes of wheat, 120 thousand metres of cloth; D: 3 lakh tonnes of wheat, 70 thousand metres of cloth; E: 4 lakh tonnes of wheat, 0 thousand metres of cloth. Find the average cost, in cloth, of each lakh tonne of wheat when the economy moves from A (all cloth) to E (all wheat).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Cloth given up from A to E = 160 − 0 = 160.
Step 2: Wheat gained = 4 − 0 = 4 lakh tonnes.
Step 3: Average cost = 160 ÷ 4 = 40. This is below the last marginal rate, 70, because the marginal rate rises.

answer.unit: thousand metres of cloth per lakh tonnes of wheat

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 40 thousand metres of cloth per lakh tonnes of wheat

questions.stem_md: The imagined economy of Belmora has the combinations of rice and steel A: 0 thousand tonnes of rice, 60 thousand tonnes of steel; B: 2 thousand tonnes of rice, 56 thousand tonnes of steel; C: 4 thousand tonnes of rice, 48 thousand tonnes of steel; D: 6 thousand tonnes of rice, 36 thousand tonnes of steel; E: 8 thousand tonnes of rice, 20 thousand tonnes of steel. Find the marginal rate of transformation between C and D.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: ΔX = 6 − 4 = 2 thousand tonnes of rice.
Step 2: ΔY = 48 − 36 = 12 thousand tonnes of steel.
Step 3: MRT = 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

answer.unit: thousand tonnes of steel per thousand tonnes of rice

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 6 thousand tonnes of steel per thousand tonnes of rice

questions.stem_md: For the Belmora schedule A: 0 thousand tonnes of rice, 60 thousand tonnes of steel; B: 2 thousand tonnes of rice, 56 thousand tonnes of steel; C: 4 thousand tonnes of rice, 48 thousand tonnes of steel; D: 6 thousand tonnes of rice, 36 thousand tonnes of steel; E: 8 thousand tonnes of rice, 20 thousand tonnes of steel, the economy moves from A to B. How many thousand tonnes of rice must be given up for each extra thousand tonnes of steel when the move is made in the opposite direction, from B back to A?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: From A to B, 2 thousand tonnes of rice cost 4 thousand tonnes of steel, so MRT = 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
Step 2: Going back, 4 thousand tonnes of steel are gained for 2 thousand tonnes of rice, so each thousand tonnes of steel costs 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 thousand tonnes of rice.

answer.unit: thousand tonnes of rice per thousand tonnes of steel

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 0.5 thousand tonnes of rice per thousand tonnes of steel

questions.stem_md: Kelvaria produces apples and tablets as follows: A: 0 hundred tonnes of apples, 100 thousand tablets; B: 5 hundred tonnes of apples, 95 thousand tablets; C: 10 hundred tonnes of apples, 85 thousand tablets; D: 15 hundred tonnes of apples, 70 thousand tablets; E: 20 hundred tonnes of apples, 50 thousand tablets. Find the marginal rate of transformation between B and C.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: ΔX = 10 − 5 = 5 hundred tonnes of apples.
Step 2: ΔY = 95 − 85 = 10 thousand tablets.
Step 3: MRT = 10 ÷ 5 = 2.

answer.unit: thousand tablets per hundred tonnes of apples

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 2 thousand tablets per hundred tonnes of apples

questions.stem_md: Using the Kelvaria schedule A: 0 hundred tonnes of apples, 100 thousand tablets; B: 5 hundred tonnes of apples, 95 thousand tablets; C: 10 hundred tonnes of apples, 85 thousand tablets; D: 15 hundred tonnes of apples, 70 thousand tablets; E: 20 hundred tonnes of apples, 50 thousand tablets, find the average number of thousand tablets given up per hundred tonnes of apples when apple output rises from B to D.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Tablets given up = 95 − 70 = 25 thousand.
Step 2: Apples gained = 15 − 5 = 10 hundred tonnes.
Step 3: Average = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5. The two marginal rates, 2 and 3, average 2.5 for equal steps.

answer.unit: thousand tablets per hundred tonnes of apples

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 2.5 thousand tablets per hundred tonnes of apples

questions.stem_md: Tarvania's frontier is A: 0 lakh tonnes of wheat, 160 thousand metres of cloth; B: 1 lakh tonnes of wheat, 150 thousand metres of cloth; C: 2 lakh tonnes of wheat, 120 thousand metres of cloth; D: 3 lakh tonnes of wheat, 70 thousand metres of cloth; E: 4 lakh tonnes of wheat, 0 thousand metres of cloth, with cloth falling smoothly as wheat rises. During a slump the economy produces 2 lakh tonnes of wheat and 90 thousand metres of cloth. How many more thousand metres of cloth could it produce, with no loss of wheat, if all resources were fully and efficiently used?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: On the frontier, 2 lakh tonnes of wheat go with 120 thousand metres of cloth.
Step 2: Idle capacity = 120 − 90 = 30 thousand metres of cloth.

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 30 thousand metres of cloth

questions.stem_md: Tarvania's frontier gives 120 thousand metres of cloth at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat. After a rise in resources and better technology the new frontier gives the maximum of 200 thousand metres of cloth with no wheat and 5 lakh tonnes of wheat with no cloth, and passes through 168 thousand metres of cloth at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat. By how many thousand metres of cloth has the economy's capacity grown at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: New cloth at 2 lakh tonnes of wheat = 168.
Step 2: Old cloth at the same wheat = 120.
Step 3: Gain = 168 − 120 = 48 thousand metres.

marking_scheme.step: Correct answer: 48 thousand metres of cloth

questions.stem_md: The maximum cloth Tarvania can produce rises from 160 to 200 thousand metres after growth. By what per cent has the maximum output of cloth risen?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Rise = 200 − 160 = 40 thousand metres.
Step 2: Per cent rise = 40 ÷ 160 × 100 = 25.

questions.stem_md: Farmer Dilbag of Bhavpur earns Rs 60,000 from sugarcane, Rs 52,000 from paddy or Rs 48,000 from vegetables on his two hectares. He chooses sugarcane. Find the opportunity cost of his choice in rupees.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The alternatives given up are paddy (Rs 52,000) and vegetables (Rs 48,000).
Step 2: The next best alternative is paddy, so the opportunity cost is Rs 52,000.

questions.stem_md: Dilbag can harvest his field with 40 workers for 5 days at Rs 400 per worker per day, or hire a harvesting machine for 2 days at Rs 30,000 per day. By how many rupees is the capital-intensive method cheaper?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Labour cost = 40 × 5 × 400 = Rs 80,000.
Step 2: Machine cost = 2 × 30000 = Rs 60,000.
Step 3: Difference = 80000 − 60000 = Rs 20,000.

questions.stem_md: What is scarcity? Why does it make choice unavoidable for the imagined island economy of Marrow?
questions.solution_md: Scarcity: limited resources, many wants; alternative uses force choice.

answer.model_answer_md: Scarcity means that the resources available are limited compared with the wants to be satisfied. Marrow cannot meet all its wants, and since its land, labour and funds have alternative uses, using them for one purpose means giving up another. This forces it to choose.

marking_scheme.step: Link with alternative uses and choice

questions.stem_md: Distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics, giving one imagined example of each from the economy of Kelvaria.
questions.solution_md: Micro: individual units; macro: the whole economy; with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Microeconomics studies individual units such as a consumer, a producer or a single market, for example how the price of tablets is set in one market. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, for example the general price level or total employment of Kelvaria.

questions.stem_md: Classify as positive or normative, with a reason: (i) "Cloth output in Tarvania rose last year." (ii) "Tarvania should tax luxury cloth heavily."
questions.solution_md: (i) positive, testable; (ii) normative, value judgement.

answer.model_answer_md: Statement (i) is positive because it describes what is and can be checked against data on cloth output. Statement (ii) is normative because the word should expresses a value judgement about what ought to be done, which facts alone cannot settle.

questions.stem_md: Define opportunity cost. What is the opportunity cost for Dilbag of Bhavpur of growing sugarcane (Rs 60,000) when paddy would bring Rs 52,000 and vegetables Rs 48,000?
questions.solution_md: Definition; next best alternative paddy, Rs 52,000.

answer.model_answer_md: Opportunity cost means the worth of the best alternative given up when one option is chosen. For Dilbag the next best use of the land is paddy, so the opportunity cost of growing sugarcane is Rs 52,000.

questions.stem_md: Define the production possibility frontier of the imagined economy of Belmora, which makes rice and steel.
questions.solution_md: Combinations of two goods, given resources and technology, full and efficient use.

answer.model_answer_md: The production possibility frontier of Belmora shows the different combinations of rice and steel that the economy can produce with its given resources and technology when the resources are fully and efficiently used. Every point on the curve is an efficient combination.

marking_scheme.step: Given resources and technology, full and efficient use

questions.stem_md: State any four assumptions behind the production possibility frontier of an imagined two-good economy.
questions.solution_md: Fixed resources, given technology, full and efficient use, not equally efficient resources.

answer.model_answer_md: The frontier assumes that the resources of the economy are fixed, that technology is given, that the resources are fully and efficiently used, and that the resources are not equally efficient in producing both goods. If any of these changes, the frontier changes.

questions.stem_md: What does it mean when the imagined economy of Lumeria is producing at a point inside its frontier, and why can it not produce at a point outside it?
questions.solution_md: Inside: underuse of resources; outside: unattainable.

answer.model_answer_md: A point inside the frontier means that some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, so the output of at least one good could be raised. A point outside is beyond what the given resources and technology can produce, so it is unattainable.

marking_scheme.step: Outside: unattainable with given resources and technology

questions.stem_md: State the formula for the marginal rate of transformation and find it between A and B for Lumeria's schedule A: 0 thousand bicycles, 50 thousand sewing machines; B: 2 thousand bicycles, 48 thousand sewing machines; C: 4 thousand bicycles, 42 thousand sewing machines; D: 6 thousand bicycles, 32 thousand sewing machines; E: 8 thousand bicycles, 18 thousand sewing machines.
questions.solution_md: MRT between A and B is 1.

answer.model_answer_md: MRT = ΔY ÷ ΔX, the units of one good given up per extra unit of the other. From A to B, 2 thousand sewing machines are given up for 2 thousand bicycles, so MRT = 2 ÷ 2 = 1.

questions.stem_md: Explain the problem of how to produce, using Dilbag's choice between 40 hired workers for 5 days and a machine hired for 2 days.
questions.solution_md: Technique choice; labour Rs 80,000 versus machine Rs 60,000.

answer.model_answer_md: How to produce is the choice of technique. Dilbag may use a labour-intensive method, costing Rs 80,000, or a capital-intensive method, costing Rs 60,000. He compares the costs and the output and selects the technique that suits him better.

marking_scheme.step: Problem identified as choice of technique

questions.stem_md: Explain the problem of for whom to produce, with the imagined economy of Dunmere in mind.
questions.solution_md: Distribution of output among people.

answer.model_answer_md: For whom to produce is the problem of distributing the output among the members of the economy. Dunmere must decide who will receive the goods and services it produces, for example the share going to workers, owners and the needy, since people with more income can buy more.

marking_scheme.step: Link with income or share of groups

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a centrally planned economy from a market economy by describing who takes the central decisions in each. Name the third type and describe it briefly.
questions.solution_md: Planned: authority decides; market: prices decide; mixed: both.

answer.model_answer_md: In a centrally planned economy a central authority takes the decisions on what, how and for whom to produce, following a plan. In a market economy buyers and sellers take them through markets and prices. A mixed economy combines both, with private firms working through markets and the government playing a role in production and regulation.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three central problems of an economy by taking the imagined economy of Kelvaria, which can produce apples and tablets.
questions.solution_md: What, how, for whom, applied to Kelvaria.

answer.model_answer_md: What to produce: Kelvaria must choose how many apples and how many tablets to make. How to produce: it must choose between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques for each. For whom to produce: it must decide how the apples and tablets will be shared among its households. These problems arise from scarcity and alternative uses.

questions.stem_md: The frontier of Kelvaria's apples and tablets is concave to the origin, with marginal rates 1, 2, 3, 4 along A: 0 hundred tonnes of apples, 100 thousand tablets; B: 5 hundred tonnes of apples, 95 thousand tablets; C: 10 hundred tonnes of apples, 85 thousand tablets; D: 15 hundred tonnes of apples, 70 thousand tablets; E: 20 hundred tonnes of apples, 50 thousand tablets. Explain why.
questions.solution_md: Increasing marginal opportunity cost because resources are not equally efficient.

answer.model_answer_md: The marginal rate rises from 1 to 4, so each extra hundred tonnes of apples costs more tablets. Resources are not equally efficient in both goods: the best orchard land and workers are used first for apples, later ones are less suited and are taken from tablet making. So the opportunity cost rises and the curve is concave.

marking_scheme.step: Rising marginal rate with the figures
Resources not equally efficient in both goods

questions.stem_md: The imagined economy of Lumeria has the schedule A: 0 thousand bicycles, 50 thousand sewing machines; B: 2 thousand bicycles, 48 thousand sewing machines; C: 4 thousand bicycles, 42 thousand sewing machines; D: 6 thousand bicycles, 32 thousand sewing machines; E: 8 thousand bicycles, 18 thousand sewing machines. Find the marginal rate of transformation for each move and state whether it rises.
questions.solution_md: MRT: 1, 3, 5, 7; it rises.

answer.model_answer_md: A to B: 2 ÷ 2 = 1; B to C: 6 ÷ 2 = 3; C to D: 10 ÷ 2 = 5; D to E: 14 ÷ 2 = 7. The marginal rates 1, 3, 5, 7 rise at every step, so the opportunity cost of bicycles increases and the frontier is concave to the origin.

questions.stem_md: State two causes of a rightward shift and one cause of a leftward shift of the production possibility frontier of the imagined economy of Orlin, and explain what each shows.
questions.solution_md: Right: more resources, better technology; left: destruction.

answer.model_answer_md: A rightward shift occurs when Orlin's resources increase, such as new labour or capital, or when its technology improves; both raise the maximum possible output, which shows economic growth. A leftward shift occurs when resources are destroyed, for example by an earthquake or flood, lowering what Orlin can produce.

marking_scheme.step: Two causes of a rightward shift

questions.stem_md: Explain how scarcity, choice and opportunity cost are connected, using the imagined town of Halsey that has one empty plot and wishes to build either a school or a hospital.
questions.solution_md: Scarcity forces choice; the forgone use is the opportunity cost.

answer.model_answer_md: Halsey has one plot, a scarce resource, with two possible uses, so it must choose. If it builds the school, the hospital cannot be built on that plot. The hospital forgone is the opportunity cost of the school. Without scarcity, both could be built and no choice or cost would arise.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics, and between positive and normative economics, giving one imagined example of each from the economy of Quillon.
questions.solution_md: Micro versus macro and positive versus normative, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Microeconomics studies individual units, such as a household, a firm or a single market; the price of tea in one Quillon market is an example. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, such as national income, total employment and the general price level; the total employment of Quillon is an example. Positive economics deals with what is, through statements that can be tested with facts, for example that tea output rose last year. Normative economics deals with what ought to be and rests on value judgements, for example that Quillon should subsidise tea growers.

questions.stem_md: The imagined economy of Lumeria can produce the combinations A: 0 thousand bicycles, 50 thousand sewing machines; B: 2 thousand bicycles, 48 thousand sewing machines; C: 4 thousand bicycles, 42 thousand sewing machines; D: 6 thousand bicycles, 32 thousand sewing machines; E: 8 thousand bicycles, 18 thousand sewing machines. Find the marginal rate of transformation for each move, state what happens to it, and explain the shape of the frontier.
questions.solution_md: MRT 1, 3, 5, 7; rising; concave.

answer.model_answer_md: For each move MRT = ΔY ÷ ΔX: A to B, 2 ÷ 2 = 1; B to C, 6 ÷ 2 = 3; C to D, 10 ÷ 2 = 5; D to E, 14 ÷ 2 = 7. The marginal rate rises at every step, so each extra thousand bicycles costs more sewing machines. This happens because resources are not equally efficient in both goods. Rising marginal opportunity cost makes the frontier concave to the origin.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: resources not equally efficient, concave frontier

questions.stem_md: Explain, with reference to the imagined economy of Tarvania, how the production possibility frontier shifts or rotates when resources and technology change.
questions.solution_md: Right, left, rotation, with causes.

answer.model_answer_md: If Tarvania's resources grow or its technology improves for both wheat and cloth, the whole frontier shifts to the right, showing growth. If an earthquake or flood destroys resources, the frontier shifts to the left. If technology improves for one good only, say cloth, the frontier rotates: the cloth intercept rises while the wheat intercept stays the same. In each case the economy can produce a different set of combinations from before.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three central problems of an economy with the imagined economy of Dunmere in mind, and say how the production possibility frontier helps to illustrate them.
questions.solution_md: What, how, for whom; the frontier shows choice, inefficiency and growth.

answer.model_answer_md: Dunmere must decide what to produce and in what quantities, because its resources are scarce and have alternative uses. It must decide how to produce, choosing a labour-intensive or capital-intensive technique. It must decide for whom to produce, that is how output is distributed among its people. The frontier shows the first problem as a choice of one point among many on the curve, and shows how resources can be wasted when the economy is inside the curve. A shift of the frontier shows growth.

marking_scheme.step: Choice of a point on the frontier

questions.stem_md: Describe the three types of economy, centrally planned, market and mixed, in terms of how each solves the central problems, using the imagined economies of Orlin, Quillon and Dunmere.
questions.solution_md: Planned: authority; market: prices; mixed: both.

answer.model_answer_md: In Orlin, a centrally planned economy, the government decides what, how and for whom to produce and owns most resources. In Quillon, a market economy, buyers and sellers decide through markets and prices, producers following profit and consumers their incomes. In Dunmere, a mixed economy, private firms and the government both take part: markets guide much of the production while the state provides services and regulates. Each type answers the same three problems, but by a different decision maker.

marking_scheme.step: Link with the three central problems

questions.stem_md: Tarvania's frontier passes through A: 0 lakh tonnes of wheat, 160 thousand metres of cloth; B: 1 lakh tonnes of wheat, 150 thousand metres of cloth; C: 2 lakh tonnes of wheat, 120 thousand metres of cloth; D: 3 lakh tonnes of wheat, 70 thousand metres of cloth; E: 4 lakh tonnes of wheat, 0 thousand metres of cloth. Explain what the points (2 lakh tonnes of wheat, 90 thousand metres of cloth) and (3, 100) show, and what the first point says about unemployment.
questions.solution_md: Inside point: 30 idle; outside point: 30 beyond the frontier.

answer.model_answer_md: At 2 lakh tonnes of wheat the frontier gives 120 thousand metres of cloth, so 90 lies inside the frontier by 30: the point is attainable but resources are unemployed or inefficiently used, and 30 more cloth could be made with no loss of wheat. At 3 lakh tonnes of wheat the frontier gives 70, so 100 is 30 beyond it and is unattainable with present resources and technology. Moving to the frontier removes unemployment; reaching beyond needs growth.

marking_scheme.step: Frontier values at the two wheat levels
Remedies: move to the frontier; growth needed
